newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scientists map policy for 21st century.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scientists map policy for 21st century.

text.p: Top U.S. scientists Wednesday laid out a blueprint for science and public policy in the 21st century, emphasising better education, measurable quality and wise prioritization in an era of limited resources.

The set of six "Preparing for the 21st Century" reports were issued by the National Academy of Sciences, the National Research Council, the National Academy of Engineering and the Institute of Medicine, prestigious groups that serve as advisers to the government on a wide range of issues.
National Academy of Sciences president Bruce Alberts told reporters the goal was to ensure that "science and technology were recognised as the driving force for the next century."

"From antibiotics to electricity to semiconductors and electronic mail, science and engineering have served as fundamental agents of improving the quality of life in our society," the presidents of the academies said.

"As we move forward into the next century, focused attention must be paid to the importance of the science and engineering enterprise," they added, introducing the reports which synthesized research and reports produced by the academies in recent years.
The reports addressed the changing health care system, the environment, engineering, education, technology and the role the behavioural sciences can play in shaping policy.
Although the final figures on U.S. government spending on science will be determined in the coming budget battle in Congress, scientists say a 20 percent cut by 2002 is possible, maybe even probable.
Therefore, more of an effort will have to be made to prioritize and to measure and quantify the quality of the work and the results they produce.

In addition, funds should be allocated to specific projects and scientists, not just to institutions. And there should be ongoing attempts to measure U.S. performance against other countries, the report said.
"We must prioritize and use merit review everywhere," said William Wulf, president of the engineering academy.

The scientists also stressed the need for the country to make better use of the masses of behavioural sciences data, which could be applied to topics as varied as understanding the impact of poverty on childhood learning to figuring out how to combat teenage smoking.

The scientists also underscored their concern about inadequate education and training, noting that a recent international survey showed U.S. eighth graders were below average in math and just slightly above average in science.
"I wonder how America would react if the Olympics were that way," Alberts said.

The academy's recommendations often make their way into public policy, although the process can be slow. For instance, food safety recommendations made 10 years ago were finally put into effect this month.

Alberts noted that even small changes can be slow in coming. He noted that he had been working without success for three years to get something healthier on the breakfast menu than the cinnamon rolls and chocolate cake he was able to offer reporters at Wednesday's breakfast briefing.
